questions.q: What is automotive testing?
options: Software and systems testing applied to ECUs, the 70–150+ small computers in a vehicle
questions.explain: General testing principles still apply.

questions.q: What three things does automotive add to general testing?
options: ECUs talking over shared buses, hardware in the loop, and safety standards with legal teeth
questions.explain: ISO 26262 and ISO 21434 apply.

questions.q: Why does a tester think in terms of bus messages?
options: Dozens of ECUs cooperate over CAN/LIN/Ethernet, so a bug can span ECUs
questions.explain: Not just function calls.

questions.q: What does the V-model connect?
options: Development activities on the left to increasingly integrated test levels on the right (unit, integration, system, acceptance)
questions.explain: Horizontal arrows say 'this test verifies that activity'.

questions.q: Why a shared bus instead of point-to-point wiring?
options: With 70–150+ ECUs, wiring every pair needs an unserviceable harness; CAN uses one pair of wires (CAN_H and CAN_L)
questions.explain: Every node listens and can transmit.

questions.q: Why does differential signalling tolerate noise?
options: Noise hits both wires equally and cancels when the receiver reads the difference
questions.explain: Important in noisy vehicles.

questions.q: What is the termination rule?
options: 120 Ω at both ends (about 60 Ω across the bus); missing or duplicate termination is a common fault
questions.explain: Check termination before blaming software when scope signals look reflected.

questions.q: Dominant versus recessive?
options: Dominant (logical 0) is actively driven and always wins; recessive (logical 1) is the passive state
questions.explain: This one fact explains arbitration.

questions.q: What does a classic CAN data frame carry?
options: SOF, arbitration (ID), control (DLC), data (0–8 bytes), CRC, ACK and EOF
questions.explain: Every tool is a view onto these bits.

questions.q: Does a CAN frame carry a destination address?
options: No: an identifier describing what the data is; each node filters
questions.explain: You observe and inject on the shared bus.

questions.q: What do arbitration and acknowledgment fall out of?
questions.explain: Lower ID wins arbitration.

questions.q: What's the data field size in classic CAN?
questions.explain: CAN FD allows more.

questions.q: What three roles does CANoe play at once?
options: Simulation (act as missing ECUs), analysis (trace, decode, timing, bus load) and stimulation/test execution
questions.explain: One PC with a Vector interface connected to the bus.

questions.q: Why simulate other ECUs?
options: Early in development or on a bench most neighbouring ECUs don't exist, or you don't want to risk expensive prototypes
questions.explain: The ECU under test believes it's on a complete network.

questions.q: What does a database (DBC/ARXML) provide?
options: Maps raw CAN IDs and bytes to named, scaled signals
questions.explain: Used to decode raw bytes in the trace.

questions.q: What does the lesson state about CANoe?
options: It's commercial software the course can't run, so it describes documented capabilities as a conceptual map
questions.explain: Use vendor training when you have access.

questions.q: What is CAPL's execution model?
options: A collection of event procedures invoked by CANoe's runtime, not a single main()
questions.explain: C-like syntax, event-driven.

questions.q: What does `on message SensorNodeStatus` do?
options: Runs every time a frame matching that message arrives, with `this` referring to it
questions.explain: Matched by symbolic name or raw ID.

questions.q: What does `on start` do?
options: Fires once at the beginning of a measurement: initialise variables, arm timers, send an initial state
questions.explain: on preStart and on stopMeasurement are setup/teardown.

questions.q: How do timers work?
options: Declare an msTimer, start it with setTimer(), and `on timer` fires once when it expires
questions.explain: The lesson notes snippets weren't run on live CANoe.

questions.q: What is UDS?
options: Unified Diagnostic Services (ISO 14229), the request/response diagnostic protocol ECUs speak
questions.explain: Client-server: tester requests, ECU responds.

questions.q: What does a positive response's SID look like?
questions.explain: It makes responses unmistakable.

questions.q: What shape does a negative response have?
options: 0x7F, the request SID, then an NRC
questions.explain: NRC is the negative response code.

questions.q: Which SID reads a live value by identifier, and which keeps a session alive?
options: 0x22 Read Data By Identifier; 0x3E Tester Present
questions.explain: 0x27 is Security Access seed/key.

questions.q: What is HIL testing?
options: A real physical ECU connected to a simulated environment (sensors, actuators, other ECUs, electrical environment) without a real vehicle
questions.explain: It's the dominant system-test technique.

questions.q: What does HIL add beyond bench network testing?
options: Physical realism: sensor curves, actuator loads, supply transients and physical faults like a shorted wire
questions.explain: A pure CAN simulation can't represent them.

questions.q: Why is HIL the sweet spot?
options: Real enough that the ECU can't tell it isn't in a vehicle, yet fully controllable and repeatable, at lower cost and safety risk
questions.explain: You can deliberately break things safely.

questions.q: What runs the plant model in a rig?
options: A real-time simulation computer with a guaranteed fixed cycle (commonly 1 ms or faster)
questions.explain: The course describes architecture, not hands-on operation.

questions.q: What's partitioned in ECU test design?
options: Signal ranges: the physical values a CAN signal, DID or sensor input can carry
questions.explain: Each case specifies the bus-level or diagnostic representation too.

questions.q: With a 120 °C overheat threshold ('above 120'), what are the four partitions of CoolantTemp (−40 to 150 °C)?
options: Below −40 invalid, −40..120 normal, >120..150 overheat, above 150 invalid
questions.explain: Representative values: −45, 90, 135, 155.

questions.q: Which boundary values do you test for 'strictly greater than 120'?
questions.explain: 120.0 is where a > versus >= bug lives.

questions.q: Why not sweep every 16-bit raw value?
options: It's impossible and pointless once you've reasoned about which values behave alike
questions.explain: Equivalence partitioning needs one representative per class.

questions.q: What are the two standards behind much automotive rigour?
questions.explain: ISO 21434 (cybersecurity) comes in Level 4.

questions.q: What are ASPICE capability levels 0 to 5?
options: Incomplete, performed, managed, established, predictable, innovating
questions.explain: Most OEM contracts target level 2 or 3.

questions.q: Which ASPICE processes are testing-relevant?
options: SWE.4 unit verification, SWE.5 integration test, SWE.6 qualification test, and SYS.4/SYS.5 system levels
questions.explain: The course practices map onto them.

questions.q: Why is ASPICE 'as much a commercial gate as a technical one'?
options: OEMs require a specific capability level from suppliers as a condition of business
questions.explain: Traceability and documented results become obligations.

questions.q: When does the fuel node raise and clear LowFuelWarning?
questions.explain: warningActive holds the hysteresis state.

questions.q: What does the DiagnosticResetRequest do?
options: Resets the node's alive counter to 0, standing in for a UDS-style diagnostic trigger
questions.explain: Received, not sent, by the node.

questions.q: How often does FuelLevelStatus transmit?
options: Every 100 ms, with FuelLevelPct, LowFuelWarning and a 4-bit AliveCounter
questions.explain: A msTimer cycleTimer drives it.

questions.q: How honest is the project about verification?
options: It was reviewed for accuracy against CAPL conventions but not compiled or run in live CANoe
questions.explain: Treat it as a template to adapt.

questions.q: What does CAPL lack compared with C?
options: Pointers and dynamic memory: every array is fixed-size and declared up front
questions.explain: Functions return void, int, long, float, byte, char[] or a message.

questions.q: What does `this.byte(i)` give?
options: A raw payload byte by index, regardless of whether a database defines signals
questions.explain: The fallback for diagnostics, unknown traffic and checksum/CRC routines.

questions.q: What is a system variable (sysvar)?
options: State shared across the whole CANoe configuration
questions.explain: Used for panels and cross-node state.

questions.q: What does the additive checksum example compute?
questions.explain: Many real ECUs use CRC8 or CRC16 with the same calling convention.

questions.q: Why use a test module instead of a simulation node?
options: It produces a structured verdict (Pass/Fail/Inconclusive) and report, which makes suites auditable and machine-consumable for CI
questions.explain: write() text can't answer 'did it pass?'.

questions.q: What does `testStepFail(...)` do?
options: Records a failing step verdict with a message
questions.explain: testStepPass records a pass.

questions.q: What does testWaitForTimeout(500) do?
options: Blocks up to 500 ms waiting for the next assertion
questions.explain: Used in the startup sequence example.

questions.q: What does testCaseTitle give?
options: A human-readable name for the case in the report
questions.explain: Test cases roll up into a report.

questions.q: What's the max payload in CAN-FD versus classic CAN?
questions.explain: The data phase can run at 5–8 Mbit/s.

questions.q: What is the byte length for DLC 13 in CAN-FD?
What new control bits does CAN-FD add?
options: FDF (FD format), BRS (bit-rate switch) and ESI (error state indicator)
questions.explain: BRS switches to the faster data-phase rate.

questions.q: What happens to the arbitration bit rate?
options: Unchanged, up to 1 Mbit/s; only the data phase speeds up
questions.explain: CRC grows to 17 or 21 bits.

questions.q: What is LIN's topology?
options: Master/slave: the master owns a schedule table of when every message is sent
questions.explain: A low-cost bus for simple devices.

questions.q: What does a LIN header consist of?
options: Break (≥13 bit-times low), Sync 0x55 and the Protected ID
questions.explain: The PID is a 6-bit ID plus 2 parity bits.

questions.q: What does the Sync field 0x55 do?
options: Lets slaves calibrate their baud rate
questions.explain: Sent by the master.

questions.q: Classic versus enhanced checksum?
options: Classic covers data only; enhanced covers data plus the PID, depending on LIN version
questions.explain: Sent by the node that provides the data.

questions.q: What does the DTC status byte's confirmedDTC bit (bit 3) mean?
options: The fault met confirmation criteria: the 'real' stored DTC
questions.explain: pendingDTC (bit 2) means failed but not yet confirmed.

questions.q: What does testFailed (bit 0) mean?
options: The fault is failing right now, this operation cycle
It failed since the last clear
questions.explain: testFailedSinceLastClear is bit 5.

questions.q: What is bit 7 warningIndicatorRequested?
options: Whether the malfunction indicator lamp should be on because of this DTC
questions.explain: Lamp state follows DTC status.

questions.q: What do the testNotCompleted bits mean?
options: The diagnostic test hasn't run since the last clear or this operation cycle
questions.explain: Absence of a failure isn't proof the test ran.

questions.q: Which DBC blocks define nodes, messages and signals?
options: BU_ nodes, BO_ messages, SG_ signals
questions.explain: CM_ comments often carry the real spec; VAL_ gives enumerations; BA_ attributes.

questions.q: A signal has scale 1, offset −40 and raw 130. What's the physical value?
questions.explain: physical = raw × 1 + (−40) = 90.

questions.q: What do @1 and @0 mean in a signal definition?
questions.explain: The sign column is + unsigned or − signed.

questions.q: Why does the valid range [-40|215] matter?
options: It's used for validation and plausibility checks
questions.explain: Raw 8-bit values 0–255 with offset −40 give −40..215.

questions.q: What does `testpreparation` do?
options: Runs once before any testcase in the module (shared setup)
questions.explain: Teardown is test completion.

questions.q: Why chain cases into sequences?
options: Shared setup/teardown and reporting that survives one case failing without aborting the whole run
questions.explain: Orchestration layer for real suites.

questions.q: What does the boundary test of 120.0 then 120.1 check?
options: Warning stays 0 at 120.0 and goes to 1 at 120.1 (strictly above)
questions.explain: testStepCheck asserts each.

questions.q: Why must cases be independent and well ordered?
options: A failure in one shouldn't corrupt the others, and state must be reset
questions.explain: Ordering and independence section.

questions.q: What is restbus simulation?
options: Simulating all the other ECUs' bus traffic around the ECU under test so it sees a complete network
questions.explain: The missing ECUs may not exist yet.

questions.q: How can a restbus be generated quickly?
options: Automatically from a DBC (cycle times and messages per node)
questions.explain: Attributes like cycle time drive transmission.

questions.q: Why is it needed at all?
options: ECUs monitor neighbours' messages and set faults or fallback modes when they're missing
questions.explain: A silent bus triggers timeout DTCs.

questions.q: What should the simulated node do besides send?
options: React to messages sent to it as the real ECU would
questions.explain: Simulation is both transmit and react.

questions.q: Where does HIL sit among test tiers?
options: Between pure simulation (nothing physical) and vehicle test (everything real): the ECU is real, the rest simulated
questions.explain: It catches defects only visible with real hardware and software.

questions.q: What does the real-time simulation computer do?
options: Runs the plant model in hard real time, completing each step within its cycle
questions.explain: Missing a cycle breaks determinism.

questions.q: What does I/O interface hardware do?
options: Converts between model values and real electrical signals the ECU expects
questions.explain: Sensor emulation and actuator loads.

questions.q: What is the ECU under test in a HIL?
options: The real, unmodified production or pre-production hardware and software
questions.explain: Bus interfaces connect it to the network.

questions.q: What are the three messages in the project?
questions.explain: Cycle times 10, 20 and 20 ms via GenMsgCycleTime.

questions.q: What does the suite validate?
options: Signal range plausibility, CAN-FD frame properties and cycle timing, with a restbus as supporting cast
questions.explain: Pulls every Level 2 module together.

questions.q: How is the 32-byte frame marked as FD?
options: A VFrameFormat attribute on the message
questions.explain: DLC 13 means 32 bytes.

questions.q: What does the restbus provide in this project?
options: The other ECUs' traffic so the ECU under test sees a complete network
questions.explain: It's the supporting cast.

questions.q: What are the two HIL automation layers?
options: A real-time layer (plant model each fixed timestep) and a test orchestration layer (what scenario, parameters, results, pass/fail)
questions.explain: The orchestration layer never touches the real-time loop's internals.

questions.q: What does 'parameterize, don't hardcode' mean for scenarios?
options: Drive scenario variations from parameters/tables instead of copying scripts
questions.explain: It scales coverage.

questions.q: What must the real-time layer guarantee?
options: Deterministic execution every fixed timestep, no exceptions
questions.explain: Examples: dSPACE or NI real-time OS.

questions.q: Which layer makes pass/fail calls?
questions.explain: It reads results.

questions.q: How do CANoe and CANape differ?
options: CANoe sees bus traffic and signals; CANape sees ECU-internal variables (RAM addresses) via XCP/CCP
questions.explain: CANoe needs a DBC; CANape needs an A2L.

questions.q: What is an A2L (ASAP2) file?
options: The map from symbol name to ECU memory address, like a DBC for calibration
questions.explain: It describes internal symbols and addresses.

questions.q: Which two A2L categories matter for testing?
options: MEASUREMENT (read live values) and CHARACTERISTIC (calibration parameters)
questions.explain: Only measurement is read-only.

questions.q: Which protocol does CANape use?
questions.explain: Over CAN or Ethernet.

questions.q: Why Ethernet in vehicles?
options: CAN tops out around 1 Mbit/s (5 for CAN-FD data phase); vehicle Ethernet runs 100 Mbit/s to multi-gigabit for cameras, radar and infotainment
questions.explain: ADAS and infotainment need the bandwidth.

questions.q: What's automotive Ethernet's physical layer?
options: 100BASE-T1 / 1000BASE-T1: a single unshielded twisted pair, chosen to cut harness weight and cost
questions.explain: Office Ethernet uses 100BASE-TX.

questions.q: What is SOME/IP?
options: An AUTOSAR-standard service-oriented middleware over IP, with services and methods
questions.explain: CAN signals are static; Ethernet comms are often service-oriented.

questions.q: Which protocols ride on automotive Ethernet?
options: SOME/IP, DoIP (diagnostics) and AVB/TSN for time-sync media
questions.explain: TCP/IP underneath.

questions.q: What is ASIL?
options: Automotive Safety Integrity Level (QM, A–D, D strictest) assigned per hazard from severity, exposure and controllability
questions.explain: It's risk-graded, not a pass/fail badge.

questions.q: What does ASIL attach to?
options: Specific safety goals/functions, not the whole ECU
questions.explain: Higher ASIL means more rigorous traceable, reviewed verification.

questions.q: What are the three ASIL factors?
questions.explain: Each hazard is rated on all three.

questions.q: What are safety mechanisms?
options: Specific detections with safe reactions, e.g. a range check that triggers a fallback
questions.explain: You test that they work when faults occur.

questions.q: Why wrap CAPL in a framework?
options: A layer above CANoe handles sequencing, rig state, data, traceability and CI-readable reporting beyond CAPL's strengths
questions.explain: CAPL is great at driving bus traffic.

questions.q: What are the framework layers?
options: Execution core, orchestration, data layer, reporting
questions.explain: Orchestration is often Python via CANoe's COM API.

questions.q: What does driving CANoe via COM require?
options: A Windows host with CANoe installed and pywin32 (exact interface names vary by version)
questions.explain: The snippet is illustrative.

questions.q: Which report formats suit CI?
questions.explain: Machine-consumable outputs.

questions.q: What are the fault classes in the taxonomy?
questions.explain: A test plan covering only signal values misses the rest.

questions.q: Which class can CAPL alone inject?
options: Signal-level: e.g. setSignal() to an implausible value
questions.explain: Communication faults are partially possible by suppressing frames.

questions.q: What do electrical faults need?
options: A physical relay/fault-insertion unit in the HIL rig
questions.explain: Open, short to ground, short to battery.

questions.q: What do power-level faults need?
options: A programmable power supply to create sags, brownouts and ignition glitches
questions.explain: For example a glitch during a flash write.

questions.q: Which property makes a regression suite trustworthy?
options: Deterministic: same input, same result every run; a flaky suite erodes trust and is worse than none
questions.explain: Also fast enough to gate changes and independent testcases.

questions.q: How are tiers arranged?
options: Smoke (2–5 min), functional (30–60 min), full regression (hours: fault injection, HIL matrices, soak)
questions.explain: Tiering solves the speed-versus-depth tension.

questions.q: Why 'clear failure attribution'?
options: A failing name/log should point at what broke, not just 'suite failed'
questions.explain: It shortens triage.

questions.q: What does 'maintained, not just accumulated' mean?
options: Remove tests for removed features and update tests for changed behaviour
questions.explain: Otherwise the suite rots.

questions.q: What's forward versus backward traceability?
options: Forward: requirement → its tests; backward: test → the requirement(s) it verifies
questions.explain: Without backward traceability a suite accumulates orphan tests.

questions.q: What does verdict coverage measure?
options: Of covered requirements, how many have a passing latest result versus never-run or failing
questions.explain: A requirement with one failing test is very different from a passing one.

questions.q: What does ASIL-weighted coverage check?
options: For safety-relevant requirements, that the required rigour (review, test techniques) was applied
questions.explain: Higher ASIL demands more.

questions.q: Why traceability at all?
options: It lets a suite answer 'is this requirement verified?' and supports audits (ASPICE, ISO 26262)
questions.explain: The chain runs from stakeholder need to test result.

questions.q: What does SOTIF (ISO 21448) address?
options: Hazards when the system works exactly as designed but the design is insufficient for the real world
questions.explain: ISO 26262 covers malfunctions.

questions.q: Example of a SOTIF problem?
options: A radar correctly reports what it sees but fails to classify a stationary object
questions.explain: Root fix: broaden the validated operating envelope or add complementary sensing.

questions.q: What are the SOTIF areas?
options: Known safe, known unsafe, unknown unsafe, unknown safe (four areas of the operating space)
questions.explain: The goal is to shrink the unknown-unsafe area.

questions.q: For Area 1 (known safe), what's the testing goal?
options: Regression-test to keep it that way
questions.explain: Area 2 needs design restrictions.

questions.q: What feature does the project plan test?
options: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB), scoped down to one clear feature
questions.explain: Scoping keeps it concrete.

questions.q: Why list out-of-scope items with reasons?
options: It's part of the plan: it states what isn't being verified and why
questions.explain: Explicit boundaries prevent false assurance.

questions.q: What's SW-REQ-201?
options: AEB commands full braking within 150 ms of a validated imminent-collision condition (ASIL D)
questions.explain: SW-REQ-202: no activation on implausible signals.

questions.q: What does the plan trace each requirement to?
options: Test cases and ASIL, so rigour and coverage are explicit
questions.explain: From Module 8.

questions.q: How does a test strategy differ from a test plan?
options: Strategy covers the whole vehicle program and all ECUs (owned by the program test lead); a plan covers one feature or ECU
questions.explain: A testcase is one check by a test engineer.

questions.q: What backs the strategy?
options: The V-model: vehicle, system and software requirements each paired with a test level
questions.explain: Vehicle validation, multi-ECU HIL, then unit and component HIL.

questions.q: What's the strategy's central job per level?
options: Deciding what gets tested where, by whom, and with what environment
questions.explain: Including the OEM/supplier split.

questions.q: Who builds most ECUs?
options: Suppliers, so the strategy must define OEM versus supplier test responsibility
questions.explain: Typical owner varies per level.

questions.q: How does automotive CI differ from pure software CI?
options: HIL rigs are expensive and physical, so rig time caps parallelism; flaky failures may be rig wiring; rollback may mean re-flashing an ECU
questions.explain: Rig scheduling is the bottleneck.

questions.q: Why run SIL before hardware steps?
options: It's cheap and fast, filtering out failures before scarce rig time is spent
questions.explain: Software-in-the-loop catches logic problems first.

questions.q: What can a flaky failure be?
options: A test problem, a rig wiring problem, or a genuine intermittent ECU defect
questions.explain: Triage needs rig health data.

questions.q: What does rig scheduling do?
options: Reserves physical rigs for jobs to avoid conflicts and maximise use
questions.explain: The pipeline queues for a rig.

questions.q: Why test cascading faults, not just single faults?
options: A mechanism proven for fault A alone and fault B alone may fail when both occur together
questions.explain: Single-fault testing structurally can't find that.

questions.q: What is robustness testing?
options: Exercising the ECU under combinations, timing and stress to find unexpected behaviour
questions.explain: Beyond the taxonomy's single faults.

questions.q: What must a fault-injection test always do afterwards?
options: Restore the system to a known state so later tests are independent
questions.explain: Module 6's 'always restore' discipline.

questions.q: What does the second assertion in the cascading example check?
options: That the combined fault still reaches the safe state
questions.explain: Safe state under combined faults.

questions.q: What is TARA?
options: Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment: ISO 21434's structured way to find assets, threats, attack paths, impact and a CAL
questions.explain: The cybersecurity analogue of FMEA.

questions.q: What does the Cybersecurity Assurance Level (CAL) drive?
options: How much testing rigour a requirement needs, like ASIL for safety
questions.explain: Test rigour scales with risk.

questions.q: What's an example attack path?
options: A compromised infotainment unit → gateway → braking ECU if the gateway doesn't segment traffic
questions.explain: Segmentation is a countermeasure.

questions.q: What protects sensitive UDS services?
options: Security Access (0x27) seed/key, which test engineers exercise often
questions.explain: Calibration writes are protected.

questions.q: What must be versioned together?
options: DBC, A2L, ECU software build, test case source and fault-injection matrix, so they match
questions.explain: The biggest failure mode at scale is mismatched artifacts.

questions.q: What is a configuration baseline?
options: A single record naming the exact versions of all artifacts used for a result
questions.explain: For example AEB-DomainController-v2.4.1-baseline.

questions.q: Why is it needed?
options: Without it a result from six months ago is nearly meaningless
questions.explain: You can't reproduce what you can't identify.

questions.q: How should DBC, A2L and CAPL be handled?
options: Version-controlled like code, even if structured-binary
questions.explain: Non-code artifacts need version control.

questions.q: Which roles does a mature practice include?
options: Test engineer, automation/framework engineer, test architect/lead, rig/infrastructure engineer, safety/security specialist
questions.explain: Smaller teams collapse several into one person.

questions.q: Why is bus-factor sharper in this domain?
options: Scarce combined skills (CAPL, rigs, safety) sit with few people
questions.explain: Mitigations include pairing.

questions.q: How does pairing on ASIL C/D test authorship help?
options: It forces knowledge transfer as a side effect of the independent-review requirement
questions.explain: Two birds, one stone.

questions.q: What does the rig engineer maintain?
options: Physical HIL rigs, fault-injection hardware and calibration of the test equipment itself
questions.explain: A key infrastructure role.

questions.q: What's the fundamental tension?
options: The OEM needs confidence a supplier's ECU meets requirements without owning the supplier's internal process
questions.explain: ASPICE gives both sides a shared language.

questions.q: Which ASPICE processes cover software unit, integration and qualification testing?
questions.explain: SYS.4/SYS.5 cover system levels, often OEM-owned.

questions.q: Is an ASPICE capability level a pass/fail grade on CAPL tests?
options: No: you can pass every test and still score poorly if traceability and process evidence are weak
questions.explain: It assesses process maturity.

questions.q: Which work product does SWE.6 expect?
options: A traceability matrix linking requirements to qualification tests
questions.explain: From Level 3 Module 8.

questions.q: How does homologation differ from internal validation?
options: A regulator defines the requirement and failure means the vehicle can't be legally sold; evidence often needs accredited labs
questions.explain: Internal failure means delay and rework.

questions.q: Which functions are homologation-relevant?
options: Specific regulated functions: braking, lighting, emissions, certain ADAS functions
questions.explain: A courtesy light usually isn't.

questions.q: How does HIL testing support homologation?
options: Pre-homologation validation against the anticipated procedure, regression after late changes, and supporting evidence
questions.explain: It supports but doesn't replace formal testing.

questions.q: Who issues the requirements?
options: Regulatory bodies such as UN ECE or NHTSA/FMVSS
questions.explain: Market-specific.

questions.q: Which career paths does the course name?
options: Specialist (safety, cybersecurity, SOTIF), architecture/leadership, move to ECU development, systems engineering, tooling/framework specialist
questions.explain: None closes off the others later.

questions.q: Which role is often the scarcest on a team?
questions.explain: Deep automation and infrastructure skill.

questions.q: What signals readiness for Senior Test Engineer?
options: Independently designing a fault-injection matrix or similar Level 3 work
questions.explain: Evidence beats tenure.

questions.q: What signals readiness for Test Architect/Lead?
options: Having navigated a real supplier/OEM disagreement or built a working strategy
questions.explain: Level 4 skillset.

questions.q: What program does the capstone use?
options: A new Battery Management System (BMS) ECU with genuine safety and security content
questions.explain: Chosen as new, not carryover.

questions.q: What does SW-REQ-501 require?
options: Disconnect the pack contactor within 200 ms of detecting cell overvoltage (ASIL D)
questions.explain: SW-REQ-502 rejects implausible readings.

questions.q: What does SW-REQ-503 involve?
options: Authenticating charging-station communication before accepting a charge-current setpoint (ASIL B with a cybersecurity level)
questions.explain: Safety and security meet.

questions.q: What does the fault matrix include?
options: Mechanisms, faults tested and combined-fault cases from Level 4 Module 3
questions.explain: Scope states what's explicitly out of scope.

questions.q: Two ECUs transmit at the same instant. ECU A sends ID 0x100 and ECU B sends 0x200. Who wins arbitration?
options: ECU A: the lower ID has dominant bits first and dominant always wins; B backs off and retries
questions.explain: Arbitration falls out of the dominant/recessive rule.

questions.q: The scope shows reflected, garbled CAN signals. What do you check first?
options: Termination: 120 Ω at both ends (about 60 Ω across), since missing or duplicate termination is a common fault
questions.explain: Don't blame software before checking the physical layer.

questions.q: A CAN-FD frame has DLC 13. How many data bytes?
A signal is defined with start bit 16, length 8, scale 1, offset −40 (Intel). Raw byte 2 is 130. What is the physical value?
questions.explain: physical = raw × 1 − 40. Verified by decoding a test frame.

questions.q: A signal with scale 0.1 and raw 0x012C (300) means:
questions.explain: 300 × 0.1 = 30.0. Verified by computation.

questions.q: A UDS request is 22 F1 90. What does a positive response start with?
questions.explain: Positive response SID = request SID + 0x40; the DID is echoed. Verified with a small responder.

questions.q: What's the response to 22 12 34 when DID 0x1234 isn't supported?
questions.explain: Negative responses are 7F, the SID, then the NRC.

questions.q: What's the response to an unknown service 0x99?
questions.explain: Verified with the responder.

questions.q: Which UDS service keeps a non-default session alive?
questions.explain: 0x10 changes session; 0x3E pings.

questions.q: A CoolantTemp warning must trigger when temperature is strictly above 120 °C. Which boundary tests are best?
questions.explain: 120.0 is where > versus >= bugs hide.

questions.q: A low-fuel warning raises below 10% and clears above 15%. At 12% after having been below 10%, is the warning on?
options: Yes: hysteresis keeps it on until above 15%
questions.explain: warningActive holds the state.

questions.q: In CAPL, which handler runs each time a particular frame arrives?
questions.explain: on start fires once; on timer when a timer expires.

questions.q: Why use a CANoe test module rather than a simulation node with write()?
options: It produces structured verdicts and reports that CI and auditors can consume
questions.explain: Text in a log isn't a verdict.

questions.q: A requirement has one test case which is currently failing. What does coverage say?
options: Requirement covered but verdict not passing; verdict coverage separates covered from passing
questions.explain: Requirement coverage alone isn't enough.

questions.q: Which standard covers hazards when the system works as designed but the design is insufficient (e.g. perception limits)?
questions.explain: ISO 26262 covers malfunctions; 21434 cybersecurity.

questions.q: Why test combined (cascading) faults?
options: Mechanisms proven separately for faults A and B may still fail when both occur
questions.explain: Single-fault testing can't find that.

questions.q: A test result from six months ago can't be reproduced. What was missing?
options: A configuration baseline naming the exact DBC, A2L, ECU build, test source and fault matrix versions
questions.explain: Artifacts must be versioned together.

questions.q: A HIL rig is shared by 10 pipelines. What is the automotive-specific bottleneck?
options: Rig time: parallelism is capped by the number of physical rigs, so reservations are scheduled
questions.explain: Run SIL first to save rig time.

questions.q: An ASPICE assessor scores a supplier low although all CAPL tests pass. Why can that happen?
options: ASPICE assesses process maturity and evidence such as traceability, not just test outcomes
questions.explain: Capability levels 0–5 grade process.

challenges.title: Decode a DBC signal
challenges.prompt: Write decode(raw_bytes, start_bit, length, scale, offset) that extracts a little-endian (Intel) signal and returns physical = raw × scale + offset. Decode CoolantTemp (start 16, length 8, scale 1, offset −40) from raw byte 130, and a 16-bit signal with scale 0.1 from 0x012C.

frame = bytes([0x00, 0x00, 130, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])

challenges.solution:
def decode(raw_bytes, start_bit, length, scale, offset, little_endian=True):
    value = int.from_bytes(raw_bytes, "little" if little_endian else "big")
    raw = (value >> start_bit) & ((1 << length) - 1)
    return raw * scale + offset

frame = bytes([0x00, 0x00, 130, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])
print(decode(frame, 16, 8, 1, -40))
print(decode(bytes([0x2C, 0x01]) + bytes(6), 0, 16, 0.1, 0))
challenges.explain: A DBC maps bit position, length, endianness, scale and offset to a physical value. Verified by running the solution.

challenges.title: A tiny UDS responder
challenges.prompt: Write respond(req) for three services: 0x10, 0x22 (Read Data By Identifier with DID 0xF190 = a VIN) and 0x3E. Positive response = SID + 0x40 (for 0x22 echo the DID then the data). Unknown service: 7F SID 11. Unknown DID: 7F 22 31. Print each response as hex.
challenges.explain: UDS positive responses add 0x40 to the SID; negative responses are 0x7F, the SID and an NRC. Verified by running the solution.
